title: About
text:
I graduated from Williams College in 2023 with a double major in computer science and math. After my undergraduate education, I spent a year in Spain teaching computer science, among other topics, at a vocational school. I’ve also had the good fortune to join batches at the Recurse Center in summer of 2022 and fall of 2024 in which I spent time building out a number of projects, like these!
Last year, I helped out in the Michigan Dems 2024 campaign, writing some texting scripts and mostly organzing volunteer door-knockers and phone bankers. More recently I worked as a maintainer for an in-house Student Information Service for a local high school, which entailed a full-stack React/NextJS project deployed on Vercel.
Currently, I’m working on Python Email resources for Posit!

🔭 My role now involves the exploration and development of resources for email in Python!
🔭 I had previously been working on a supplemental Great Tables package called gt-extras!
🌱 I’m currently learning how to toy around with R Shiny apps, one of which can be found here.
💬 I’m looking to collaborate on gt-extras, please submit issues and PR’s!
👯 I spend my time climbing, playing soccer and table tennis, and volunteering at a weekly legal clinic.

title: Great Tables & gt-extras: Talk Outline
text:
Duration: 35 minutes + 5 min Q&A






Slide: Title Slide - Title: “Great Tables & gt-extras” - Subtitle: “Telling Better Data Stories with Beautiful Tables”
Slide: About You - 📊 gt-extras author, Great Tables contributor - 💡 I enjoy patterns and helping people see patterns - Who am I to tell you about tables? (Personal connection: KenKen puzzle image. emphasize that tables, like puzzles, are a great place to see patterns.)
Slide: The Problem - Show a screenshot of a plain, ugly table (default pandas DataFrame display) - Quote: “They say a picture is worth a thousand words, so why do we have to look at tables with a thousand cells of text?” - The belief we’re challenging: “Tables are boring. Charts tell the real stories.” - Our argument: Tables CAN be beautiful, engaging, AND tell powerful stories







Slide: Full NFL Table - Show the complete rendered NFL 2011 season table (from current slides) - Take a moment to let it sink in: This is a table, but it’s visually engaging - It tells multiple stories at once
Slide: What Makes It Work? - Strategic use of color (green/yellow/red for point differential) - Embedded visualizations (win/loss streaks, dumbbell plots) - Clear hierarchy and organization (division grouping, team logos) - Responsive styling (Super Bowl winners highlighted) - Professional theme/polish
Slide: This Wasn’t Hand-Coded HTML - This was created with Python + Great Tables + gt-extras - Clean, chainable API (show the method chaining structure without diving into code details yet) - The point: You don’t need to be a web designer to make this







Section: What is Great Tables? (7 minutes)
Slide: Great Tables Foundation - Created by Rich Iannone (originally gt in R) - Now available in Python (maintained by Michael Chow at Posit) - Philosophy: Tables are a first-class visualization medium - Key capabilities: - Organize and present data clearly - Apply professional formatting (numbers, dates, currencies) - Add titles, subtitles, source notes - Style cells, rows, columns - Create polished, publication-ready output
Slide: The Components of a Table - Show the Great Tables component diagram (visual reference from docs) - The building blocks (from top to bottom): - Table Header (optional) - Title and subtitle - Stub & Stub Head (optional) - Row labels and row groups - Column Labels (required) - Column headers, optionally with spanners - Table Body (required) - The data cells - Table Footer (optional) - Source notes and footnotes - Key insight: Think of a table as a composition of parts, not a monolith - The chainable API lets you build these parts together, each method adds clarity
Slide: Building Blocks in Action - The NFL Example - Show how each component appears in the NFL table: - Header: “NFL 2011 Season” title - Stub: Team names, organized by division (row groups) - Column Labels: Score, Wins, Losses, etc. - Body: The data, with embedded visualizations and colors - Footer: Data source attribution - Key insight: Every component serves the story. Nothing is decorative.
Slide: Structuring Your Data - The stub: Grouping rows for context (e.g., by division) - Makes patterns visible without additional explanation - Example: In NFL table, you immediately see which division won the most games - Column organization: Headers and spanners group related columns - Example: Group “Wins/Losses/Ties” under one spanner vs. separating them - Why it matters: Structure guides the reader’s eye and shapes their understanding
Slide: Formatting & Polishing - Format numbers meaningfully: - Decimals (precision matters) - Currency (for financial data) - Percentages (for proportions) - Compact notation (large numbers readable) - Example: In NFL table, points are formatted consistently - Polish with basic styling: - Colors, fonts, alignment—choose intentionally - Every choice should reduce cognitive load, not add distraction - Why it matters: Professional formatting signals “this data is important”
Slide: The Art of Visual Hierarchy - Guide attention with contrast: - Color (most powerful): Use strategically to highlight patterns - Size/weight: Headers bigger/bolder than body - Spacing: Group related items, separate concerns - Strategic use of the full table: - Headers and spanners guide the eye to structure - Stubs create visual anchors - Footer provides context (source, notes) - Example: NFL table uses color on point differential to instantly convey performance - Key insight: Every element works together to tell the story faster
Section: gt-extras - Unlocking Creative Potential (7 minutes)
Slide: What is gt-extras? - Extension package that adds powerful new capabilities to Great Tables - Built on top of the Great Tables foundation (components + formatting + styling) - Philosophy: Use tables for data storytelling, not just data presentation - The question it answers: “What if we could embed visualizations and advanced styling within table cells?” - Organized into 4 main capability areas:
Slide 1: Plotting Functions ⭐ PRIMARY FOCUS - “Put Small Multiples Inside Your Table Cells” - gt_plt_bar() - Embed bar charts in cells (compare magnitudes) - gt_plt_dumbbell() - Compare two values visually (before/after, actual vs. target) - gt_plt_winloss() - Show win/loss/tie records at a glance (seasons, streaks) - gt_plt_bullet() - Show performance against targets (goal tracking) - gt_plt_sparkline() - Trend visualization in cells (time series at a glance) - Why? Numbers alone obscure patterns. Let visualizations live alongside data. - Example from NFL table: Win/loss streaks and dumbbell plots (margin of victory vs. margin of defeat)
Slide 2: Coloring & Highlighting Functions - “Leverage Color as a Data Channel” - gt_color_box() - Heat map style coloring with custom palettes - gt_highlight_cols() / gt_highlight_rows() - Draw attention strategically - gt_add_divider() - Visual separation for emphasis - Why? Color is one of the fastest ways our brains process information - Cognitive science: Humans process color faster than text or even small charts - Example from NFL table: Green/yellow/red for point differential
Slide 3: Theming Functions - “Pre-Built, Professional Aesthetics” - gt_theme_538() - FiveThirtyEight style (data journalism aesthetic) - gt_theme_dot_matrix() - Playful, retro aesthetic - Pre-built themes for instant professionalism - Why? Consistency and polish matter; shouldn’t require hours of CSS - Insight: Great Tables handles the technical details; gt-extras provides the polish
Slide 4: Iconing & Imaging Functions - gt_fa_rank_change() - Font Awesome icons for trends (arrows, up/down, etc.) - fmt_image() - Embed images directly in cells (logos, photos) - Why? Visual elements are faster to parse than text - Example: NFL table uses team logos instead of team name text alone
Slide: The Real Power - Stacking Capabilities - Show the NFL example as a complete picture: - Start with a DataFrame of NFL data - Use Great Tables to structure: grouping by division (stub), organizing columns - Use Great Tables to format: team logos (images), scores (numbers) - Use Great Tables to style: basic colors and fonts - Use gt-extras to elevate: embedded win/loss streaks, dumbbell plots, color boxes - Use gt-extras theming: consistent, professional aesthetic - Each layer adds a dimension to the storytelling - The result: One cohesive, beautiful table that answers multiple questions simultaneously - Key insight: Great Tables is the foundation. gt-extras is the creative power-up.







Slide: What People Have Built (from posit-dev.github.io/gt-extras/examples/) - Showcase 3-4 different pre-rendered examples from gt-extras documentation - Show diversity of approaches: - Financial/business tables - Sports analytics - Scientific data - Creative/experimental - Message: This isn’t just for one use case; it’s a toolkit for many stories
Slide: Show 2-3 Specific Examples - Example 1: gt_plt_bar() with car data (horsepower, torque across models) - Example 2: gt_color_box() with island sizes (intuitive color gradients) - Example 3: gt_theme_dot_matrix() with air quality data (playful but professional)







Slide: 2025 Table Contest - Brief interlude: Posit Table Contest celebrates creative data visualization in tabular form - Entries showcase the full spectrum of possibility - Some use gt or gt-extras - Some use other tools (R gt, HTML, JavaScript tables, etc.) - The point: See what you might create with these tools
Slide: Contest Winner Highlight (1-2 examples) - Show a stunning example or two - Don’t dive deep—just let it inspire - Message: This is what’s possible. Your next table could be here.





Slide: The Takeaway - Tables don’t have to be boring - Great Tables + gt-extras make beautiful, functional tables accessible - Tables can tell stories as well as (or better than) charts—faster, clearer, more nuanced - You have everything you need to try this right now
Slide: Thanks + Resources - Credit: Rich Iannone, Michael Chow, and the Posit team - Links: - Great Tables: https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/ - gt-extras: https://posit-dev.github.io/gt-extras/ - Table Contest: https://posit.co/table-contest/ - Q&A invitation





Tables are underrated. They’re often faster to parse than charts.
Beauty and function go together. Polish isn’t frivolous; it signals professionalism and engages your audience.
The tools are accessible. You don’t need to be a designer or web developer.
Storytelling is the goal. Every formatting choice should serve the narrative.





Intro (Who are you): 2 min
The Problem: 2 min
Killer Example (full view): 1 min
Deconstructing the example: 5 min
What is Great Tables?: 7 min

Foundation + API: 2 min
Structuring data: 2 min
Formatting & polishing: 2 min
Visual hierarchy: 1 min

What is gt-extras?: 7 min

Overview + 4 capability areas: 4 min
The power of combining: 3 min

Examples Gallery: 4 min
Table Contest: 2 min
Closing: 1 min
Total: 31 minutes (4 min buffer for pacing/questions mid-talk)






Tone: Enthusiastic but authentic. You love patterns; tables are patterns in data.
Visuals: Rely heavily on pre-rendered examples. Let the tables speak for themselves.
Pacing: Start strong with the NFL example to show “this is possible.” Then explain the tools. Then show more possibilities.
Call to Action: Leave people wanting to try it. This is an inspiration talk, not a tutorial.




The talk follows a specific philosophy about tables as a medium: 1. Tables have components (not monolith structure) - Great Tables teaches you to think compositionally 2. Each component serves the story - Nothing is decorative; every choice guides understanding 3. Great Tables provides the foundation - Structure, formatting, styling 4. gt-extras adds creative power - Embed visualizations, leverage color, achieve polish 5. The result is data storytelling - Just as effective as (often better than) charts for communicating insights
Use this framework to guide which examples you show and how you present them. Every visual should reinforce: “Look how these components work together to tell a story.”

title: Adding Plots to Great Tables
text:
While working on gt-extras, I’ve been exploring how to add small plots to Great Tables. These can go by many names, like spark lines, nanoplots, and so on. In this post, I’ll look at three approaches I tried: adding plots with plotnine, svg.py, or adding HTML directly. In the first two cases, the plots are SVGs, while the latter entails a collection of composed HTML div elements.
Here are the pieces I’ll cover:
In the end, it’s often simplest to use svg.py, since you can create basic charts with minimal overhead. Building elements with HTML has even less overhead, but it is also slightly less user-friendly. At the other end of the spectrum, as your charts become more complex, using existing packages like the more exhaustive plotnine is a good alternative.
Animal
  Legs
  Plot



  
    Ostrich
    2
    2
  
  
    Spider
    8
    8
  
  
    Lion
    4
    4
Here is the final result:
Code
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT
from svg import SVG, Rect, Line

df = pl.DataFrame({"Animal": ["Ostrich", "Spider", "Lion"], "Legs": [2, 8, 4], "Plot": [2, 8, 4]})

width = 50
height = 30
max_legs_value = df["Legs"].max()


def create_plot_svg_py(val: int) -> str:
    canvas = SVG(
        width=width,
        height=height,
        elements=[
            Rect(
                x=0,
                y=height / 4,
                width=width * (val / max_legs_value),
                height=height / 2,
                fill="blue",
            ),

title: Adding Plots to Great Tables
text:
The Binding Component: GT.fmt()
Let’s take advantage of the fmt() method to apply a plotting function that formats our row values into plots. To see how we might use fmt(), we first need to define a formatting function to apply to each cell in a column. It will take as input the value in the cell, and should return whatever you want in that cell. Before plotting, let’s imagine we wanted to replace the number with a tally of the number of legs:

def create_leg_tally(value: int) -> str:
    return "|" * value


gt.fmt(fns=create_leg_tally, columns="Plot")

title: Adding Plots to Great Tables
text:
A Lightweight Approach: Svg.py
Now we can apply that same logic to making our plots. Let’s start with the function that will eventually be passed into fmt():

from svg import SVG, Rect, Line

height = 30
width = 50


def create_plot_svg_py(val: int) -> str:
    canvas = SVG(
        width=width,
        height=height,
        elements=[
            Rect(
                x=0,
                y=height / 4,
                width=width * (val / max_legs_value),
                height=height / 2,
                fill="blue",
            ),
            Line(x1=0, x2=0, y1=0, y2=height, stroke="black"),
        ],
    )

    html = f"<div>{canvas}</div>"
    return html

Here you get to call fmt() to modify the column you want to apply the plotting function to.

This was very direct, we didn’t have save to a buffer or import heavy duty plotting functions. We built the string with the help of svg.py and were able to insert into the table. See the string below:




'<div><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50" height="30"><rect x="0" y="7.5" width="25.0" height="15.0" fill="blue"/><line stroke="black" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="30"/></svg></div>'


Even in its outputted form the string is still easily readable, which is another upside of using an SVG generation package.

title: Adding Plots to Great Tables
Adding Plots to Great Tables
text:
A Comprehensive Package: Plotnine

from io import StringIO
from plotnine import (
    ggplot,
    aes,
    coord_flip,
    geom_col,
    scale_y_continuous,
    scale_x_continuous,
    theme_void,
    geom_hline,
)

max_legs_value = df["Legs"].max()


def create_plot_plotnine(val: int) -> str:
    plot = (
        ggplot()
        + aes(x=1, y=val)
        + geom_col(width=0.5, fill="green", show_legend=False)
        + scale_y_continuous(limits=(0, max_legs_value))
        + scale_x_continuous(limits=(0.5, 1.5))
        + coord_flip()
        + theme_void()
        + geom_hline(yintercept=0)
    )

    buf = StringIO()
    plot.save(buf, format="svg", width=0.5, height=0.3, verbose=False)
    svg_content = buf.getvalue()
    buf.close()

    html = f"<div>{svg_content}</div>"
    return html


# This might be familiar by now
gt.fmt(fns=create_plot_plotnine, columns="Plot")

Nice! But that was a sizable chunk of code just to create plots comprised of one bar each. If you’re like me, you’ll find it’s not at all trivial to do, especially without experience using the plotting package.
However, this isn’t the only graphic you might want to have on display – when you come across a use case that necessitates more detailed plots, a comprehensive plotting package like plotnine could very well be your best bet. Imagine we are passing in a list of tuples and want to generate a scatterplot, writing all of those as svg.py elements or direct HTML would be quite cumbersome.

title: Adding Plots to Great Tables
text:
Conclusion
How you choose to add plots to Great Tables is up to you. In writing graphical plotting functions for gt-extras, I’ve personally turned towards an HTML-only approach that I’ve felt comfortable with in other settings. With that said, I do believe converting table values to graphic output is a task best done with a little bit of help (whether it be svg-py or another plotting package will depend on how detailed your plots are).
The choice ultimately depends on your specific needs: simplicity and directness, versus abstraction and power. By understanding the trade-offs, you will be able to tailor your approach to the needs of your project.

title: A Great Summer of Great Tables
text:
I spent the summer working for Posit (formerly known as RStudio), and I loved it. I was on the tinytools squad, as an intern for Great Tables, the Python port of {gt} in R. My team was responsible for many of the major ports from Posit’s R packages to Python. They are awesome – this is certainly an incomplete list, but they’ve created the Python versions of {ggplot2}, {pointblank}, {scales}, {forcats}, {dplyr}, and {reactable}, to name a few.
My summer consisted of:

title: A Great Summer of Great Tables
text:
What I Did
The technical work at first largely consisted of work on my own package, an addition to the Great Tables ecosystem by way of extension. Then I was able to contribute directly to Great Tables as well, which was very satisfying. I also had the unexpected (and welcome) task of presenting and promoting my work to the open‑source community.
I also got to meet tons of folks from the wider Posit community, thanks to internal weekly matchmaking, fun talks/hangouts (and even an in-person meetup). I’ve met so many wonderful people over the past few months that I couldn’t possibly list them all here. Suffice to say that from intern hangouts to coffee chats with Posit developers in Europe, to career advice with former python open source team members, to data science talks, the remote world of my internship has not been all too remote.

gt-extras
If you’re here I’ll assume you know about the gt-extras package, or at the very least you know who I am, so I’ll avoid the shameless plug. The overwhelming majority of my work this summer has entailed a port of the {gtExtras} R package to Python, a task that was made more complex and interesting because of the underlying differences between the R and Python versions of Great Tables.





The core tasks of the gt-extras library are to:

make existing features of Great Tables easier to use
add in-cell plotting
compose styles to replicate the themes of famous publications
execute simple html and post-processing steps

Rich Iannone (one of my great mentors) got me started with the package structure, since he had already written a minimal version with one theme. That class of functions turned out to be the most bang for my buck – take the exact styling options researched and implemented by Thomas Mock in {gtExtras}, and with minimal syntax changes I had finished the themes!
But it wasn’t all copy and paste. In fact, after that, just about every function had a pretty critical deviation from the R version. The underlying dataframe in the Python package is different from R, and gtExtras had access to ggplot2, two elements that were inaccessible to me. Since we wanted to keep dependencies light, I did all of the data wrangling and graphics myself.
Michael Chow (my other great mentor) pointed me towards Narwhals (a library meant for handling different dataframe libraries). Both he and Rich encouraged me to try out different approaches to plotting, and while they could have easily told me “do it this way,” I am very grateful that I was trusted enough to make those decisions and discoveries myself.
Over the first couple of weeks, I met with both daily, and later we made longer term targets and paired for the more critical decisions. One of which was the first external contribution into my package, which was a delight to see. For the most part, I was given low-level autonomy over implementation choices, and reserved pairing for decisions like how to approach building plots or how to unify competing underlying dataframes (looking at you, Narwhals 👀). The independence was freeing, as it helped me learn what I could do myself, even when at first it felt like a good thing to ask for help on (like designing the documentation website).
Okay, fine – I can’t help but show off some of the cool things it can do. We can see a summary of the 2011 NFL season, my favorite being the winloss charts, primarily because of how much winning my New York Giants did that season.



A mega-example built with the gt-extras library




Great Tables
The very first PR I made to Great Tables was an entirely new feature, to rotate column labels 90 degrees. I don’t think I realized it at the time, but the workflow of that task was exactly how I approached the functions in gt-extras. Namely, I had to write a function, write a docstring with an example, add it to the documentation, and then write tests. This last part kind of grew on me, even though I’d embarrassingly never really done it before.
It didn’t stop there – as I progressed through styling and coloring functions, I uncovered little improvements I wanted to make to Great Tables. The bonus side effect of spending all those hours extending Great Tables is that I became perhaps the most frequent user (and tester) of the package. Eventually, I got to a point where I was fluent enough with Great Tables source code, and tacked some larger features and known bugs. So a number of my own GitHub issues (and my subsequent PRs) made their way into the repository:


a grand 😉 new feature
a collection of many different fixes to old group bugs
a row striping indexing bug with grouped data
a data coloring palette bug
an improvement to autocoloring the text of striped rows
an improvement to autocoloring in semi-transparent elements



Package Promotion
It seems obvious now, but I had never thought about what happens to a package after we write it. It’s a good thing I had Michael and Rich pushing me through this step because, had it been up to me, the world would never have learned about this package. Talking about the package doesn’t come easily to me, especially when it’s to an audience of more than just my roommate, but it really helped that the team gave me the first boost (and it certainly didn’t hurt to have the Posit organization promoting it too).
And selfishly I must admit the effect of broadcasting the package far and wide is rewarding. Seeing the package featured on a blog post, or used in someone’s repository will make my day. Because it’s so cool to know the design choices I stayed awake thinking about were (possibly) appreciated by a fellow data enthusiast.

title: A Great Summer of Great Tables
text:
What I Learned
This summer touched on so many aspects of open source code, from the technical to the collaborative. I learned how to take an idea and turn it into a fully functioning Python package, and I gained hands-on experience with the whole development workflow. Beyond the code itself, I also learned the importance of communicating my work, whether through documentation, blog posts, or presentations.

Package Development

Before this summer, I had no idea what really went into making a Python package from scratch. I learned how to set everything up, from the folder structure, to setup files, to GitHub actions and beyond. I got comfortable with things like versioning, documentation, and publishing to PyPI. Now packaging up code feels way less mysterious and way more doable.
The open process taught me to write code that is readable and maintainable, not just functional. I also gained a deeper appreciation for documentation, not just as a reference, but as a way to welcome new users and contributors.


Development Organization
With a little shame, I must admit I never knew how to use a branch. That’s an exaggeration. I knew what a branch was, and I knew to make one so I didn’t have to commit to the main branch. The shameful part is once I had a branch, all the new code went into that. (🙈 Don’t look at the repository for this website). And then one day, when I felt like there was probably too much code I hadn’t committed to the main branch, I’d merge it and ta-da, surely that was good enough… right? Fortunately, I learned about how to separate code into isolated pieces, to then merge code in a way that keeps the project organized and maintainable.
With even more shame, I have to admit I didn’t know how to write a suite of tests. Again, I knew what tests were supposed to do, but the concept seemed like something meant for more professional environments, never for code that I worked on. Until my work became code that other people could theoretically rely on – then I knew it had to be dependable. So from snapshot tests, to checking for the presence of css and html content, future changes and dependency upgrades can be relied on not to break the package.
I’m not claiming to be a pro, but thanks to Rich and Michael’s mentoring, I am now much better at adhering to these practices than I used to be.


Writing things like this!

Whether it’s a blog post for me (this one!), a blog post for Great Tables or a blog post for the entirety of Posit, I have had no shortage of opportunities to talk about my work. As you might guess, this doesn’t come naturally to me, but it’s yet another skill I’ve gotten to practice and hone in my summer at Posit.
In every instance (yes, even the slides), I’ve presented my musings using Quarto markdown. I promise I’m not getting paid to say this, but having never used Quarto before this summer, I can confidently say I can’t imagine a life without it. Life with Quarto was especially easy when the team that maintains it was part of the organization I worked for :) which I’ll definitely miss. Instead, I guess you’ll find me lurking in GitHub issues.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SummaryRowInfo:
    """Information about a single summary row"""

    id: str
    label: str  # For now, label and id are identical
    values: dict[str, str | int | float]  # TODO: consider datatype
    side: Literal["top", "bottom"]  # TODO: switch to enum
    group: GroupRowInfo


class SummaryRows(_Sequence[SummaryRowInfo]):
    """A sequence of summary rows"""

    _d: list[SummaryRowInfo]

    def __init__(self, rows: list[SummaryRowInfo] | None = None):
        self._d = []

        for row in rows or []:
            self.add_summary_row(row)
